E3: Rectifiers, Zener regulators and clippers (Week 2)

Why this matters in the exam: The Week 2 material is the single biggest chunk of the diode half of the course. The practice test gives it 10 of 50 marks directly: Q4 (5 marks) is WS3 Q13 word for word (Zener design for and ), Q5 (5 marks) is WS3 Q12 (series clipper with a battery). MCQ III (full-wave vs half-wave) adds one more mark. The formula table at the back of the test gives you , , and %V.R. It does not tell you when to use , which to use, or where the worst case is. Those decisions are where the marks are.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The power-supply chain

Transformer → rectifier → filter capacitor → regulator (Week 2 slide 24). Each stage has one job:

Stage What it does What you calculate

Filter C Holds the peak between pulses, leaves a sawtooth ripple , , , , , choose C
Zener regulator Holds fixed against supply and load changes , , , , , load range, % regulation

1.4 The Zener shunt regulator (slides 13–14)

Circuit: → → output node. The Zener (cathode up) and go from the output node to ground.

Equation Meaning
Zener model: a battery (or ) in series with . Ideal Zener: .
Current through (KVL)
KCL at the output node
Zener dissipation. Worst at no load, highest supply.

Key insight: with an ideal Zener, is fixed, so does not depend on the load. The load just decides how is shared. When goes up, goes down by the same amount. Regulation is lost when would fall below (or the knee). Your Prac 1 shows exactly this: stayed at 17.4 mA ± 2.3 % while changed by a factor of 45.

These are the Worked example 3 values. Raise the load current towards 200 mA and watch fall by the same amount while stays put, until regulation is lost.

The two worst cases (WS3 Q13, Q22):

  • Heaviest load at the lowest supply sets : .
  • Lightest load at the highest supply sets the Zener rating: and .

Line and load regulation. The course defines only %V.R. The textbook defines two small-signal measures that come straight from the model:

  • Line regulation (mV/V).
  • Load regulation (mV/mA).

Small means good regulation on both measures.

1.5 Clippers and clampers (slides 61–65)

  • Series clipper: the diode is in series with the load. is zero (or a battery level) when the diode is off.
  • Parallel clipper: the diode, with an optional battery, sits across the output. is held at the battery level ± when the diode is on, and follows when it is off.
  • The method is always the same: find the transition voltage where (or 0 for an ideal diode). Write one linear equation for in each region. Sketch directly under on the same axes.
  • Clamper: a series C with a shunt diode. The capacitor charges to the input peak through the diode, then holds it. The whole waveform shifts by that dc level, and its shape and peak-to-peak value are unchanged. With an ideal diode whose anode is at the output (cathode to ground), the output sits between and . Reverse the diode and it sits between 0 and .
  • Voltage doubler (slide 65): a clamper followed by a peak detector. charges to , so sees , which peaks at . charges to (minus two diode drops if they are not ideal). Each diode must block .

1.6 Special diodes (slides 16–17, 66)

Device Biased Key fact
LED Forward Emits light with , and . So . The eye sees roughly 350–800 nm and peaks near 550 nm. The forward drop is larger than silicon (about 1.5–3 V).
Schottky (SBD) Forward Metal on moderately doped n-type. It has a lower forward drop (about 0.3–0.5 V) and fast switching, because there is no minority-carrier storage. Good for low-voltage rectifiers.
Varactor Reverse A voltage-variable capacitor. decreases as increases, because the depletion layer widens. Used for tuning.
Photodiode Reverse Light generates electron–hole pairs in the depletion layer. The photocurrent is a reverse current proportional to light intensity.
Zener Reverse (breakdown) Conducts opposite to the arrow at . Modelled as .

Worked example 2: your Prac 1 half-wave supply (real data)

Given (from your findings summary): the adapter measured 11.11 V rms at 49.99 Hz. Si diode, V. Load 1 kΩ. Filter 47 µF, then 47 + 470 = 517 µF. Measured: unfiltered peak 15.60 V. With 47 µF and 1 kΩ: V, V, V. No load (20 kΩ bleeder only): V. With 517 µF: V, V.

Find: (a) the expected unfiltered peak; (b) the predicted ripple with 47 µF and with 517 µF; (c) the ripple factor and the C needed for < 10 %; (d) the % regulation.

(a) V, so V. You measured 15.60 V, which is 3.9 % above this prediction. The “9 V” label would predict only V. The unloaded transformer secondary sits well above its rating, so the transformer explains the difference, not the diode.

(b) Use the course’s alternate form with the measured . This avoids having to guess the sagging peak: The 517 µF prediction is good because ms ≫ ms. With 47 µF, ms is only 2.35 T, so the “” assumption behind the formula is weak. If you use V in , you get 5.65 V. The exact exponential, , gives 4.60 V, which is much closer. The capacitor’s ±20 % tolerance covers the rest.

(c) Ripple factor with 47 µF: For you need . With : cancels, so the answer does not depend on the output level. The 517 µF you fitted gives .

(d) % regulation of the unregulated half-wave supply, taking 1 kΩ as full load: After the 5.1 V Zener stage (Section B), the same definition gave at 216 Ω and at 1.78 kΩ. That is the regulator doing its job.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using instead of for a full-wave ripple. The test formula sheet prints only . For a bridge or centre-tap, the capacitor is refilled every , so you need . Write “full-wave ⇒ ” on your answer.
  • Forgetting or the diode drops. is not . A bridge loses , and centre-tap and half-wave lose .
  • Treating the ripple factor as . The course and Prac 1 define with . “10 % ripple” therefore means .
  • Calling “the average diode current”. It is the average during conduction . Over a full cycle, a half-wave diode’s dc current is just .
  • Leaving in radians when asked for a fraction or a time. Divide by for the fraction of the cycle, and by for in seconds.
  • Sizing at the wrong extreme. comes from maximum load at minimum supply. The Zener power comes from no load at maximum supply. Mixing these up loses both marks.
  • Not checking that the Zener is on. If , the Zener is off and is just the divider value. Your Prac 1 216 Ω load fell below Ω and dropped out.
  • Clippers: forgetting the battery, or drawing on different axes. Find first, label the levels, and draw under .

WS3 Q19 (course question). In the schematic below, we see the components of a typical linear DC power supply. Draw the signal at different stages of the circuit if we use half-wave or bridge rectifiers. Discuss the changes in the signal in your group. Assume that the forward voltage drop of the diode is zero.

Solution

Sketches only. 240 V ac sine → transformer: 12 V peak sine → rectifier: pulsating dc (bridge: a hump every half-cycle, at ; half-wave: one hump per cycle, at ) → capacitor: dc with a sawtooth ripple (the half-wave ripple is larger because it refills only once per cycle) → regulator: flat 5 V dc.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

RECTIFIERS   Vm = √2·Vs(rms).  Vp = Vm − VD (HW, CT)  |  Vm − 2VD (bridge)
  Vdc(no C): HW Vm/π   FW 2Vm/π    f_out: HW f, FW 2f
  PIV: HW Vs (≈2Vm WITH C) | CT 2Vs − VD | bridge Vs − VD ; rate ≥1.5×PIV
  With rf: Im = Vm/(rf+R) [bridge 2rf+R]; HW Idc=Im/π, Irms=Im/2; FW 2Im/π, Im/√2
FILTER (CR >> T)   Vr(pp) = Vp/(fCR) = IL/(fC)   FULL-WAVE: use 2f
  Design: C = Vp/(f R Vr) [or 2f].  Vo(dc) = Vp − Vr/2,  IL = Vo/R
  ωΔt = √(2Vr/Vp) rad ; fraction = ωΔt/2π ; Δt = ωΔt/(2πf)
  HW: iDav = IL(1+π√(2Vp/Vr))   iDmax = IL(1+2π√(2Vp/Vr))
  FW: iDav = IL(1+π√(Vp/2Vr))   iDmax = IL(1+2π√(Vp/2Vr))
  Ripple factor r = Vr(rms)/Vdc, Vr(rms) = Vr(pp)/(2√3) -> 10% => Vr(pp)=0.346 Vdc
  %VR = (VNL − VFL)/VFL × 100
ZENER   VZ = VZ0 + rz·IZ ;  IS = (Vs−VO)/RS = IZ + IL
  Analyse: (VO−VZ0)/rz + VO/RL = (Vs−VO)/RS ; check IZ>0 ; PZ = VO·IZ
  Design: VZ = VL ; RS = (Vs,min − VZ)/(IL,max + IZ,min)   [PT Q4: 20 Ω]
          PZ,max = VZ[(Vs,max − VZ)/RS − IL,min]  (no load!)  [PT Q4: 2.4 W]
  Load range: RL,min = VZ/(IR,min − IZ,min) ; RL,max = VZ/(IR,max − IZ,max) (∞ if ≤0)
  Line reg = (rz||RL)/(RS + rz||RL) ; Load reg = −(rz||RS)
  Filtered supply: use the ripple VALLEY Vp − Vr as Vs,min
CLIPPER: assume OFF -> vd(vi) -> set vd = VD -> viT -> vo per region -> sketch under vi
  [PT Q5: +20/−5 V square, 4 V battery opposing: vo = 0 / −1 V]
CLAMPER: C charges to Vm, waveform shifts by Vm, same p-p. DOUBLER: ≈2Vm, PIV 2Vm
